summary: This document describes evolving technology in residential networks, with more devices and more internal routing, and defines a general architecture for IPv6 home networking. It sets out principles, considerations and requirements, and highlights implications of using IPv6 at home.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7368 describes what an IPv6 home network should look like when it grows beyond one subnet behind one router. It asks for a network that configures itself, keeps working when the provider renumbers its addresses, keeps internal traffic separate from the internet, and still finds printers and other services by name. The document is a set of principles for later specifications to follow.

questions: why use ula addresses in a home network
subtitle: The principles for an IPv6 home network that has several subnets, several routers and no user configuration.

tldr.problem: Home networks are filling with devices, more of them are behind internal routers, and most of them are still single-subnet IPv4 networks behind a NAT, configured by people who are not expected to configure anything.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7368 sets out principles for an IPv6 home network: reuse existing protocols, support arbitrary topologies and several providers, delegate prefixes automatically, use Unique Local Addresses for stable internal addressing, route internally, filter at the borders, and provide naming and service discovery across the whole home.
tldr.outcome: It is a set of principles and requirements rather than a protocol. The document says that later specifications for routing, prefix management, security, naming and service discovery are expected to follow it, and it names the open questions it could not settle.

facts.label: Routing protocols at one time
facts.value: At most one unicast and one multicast

today: RFC 7368 is an Informational RFC published in October 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is a set of principles and requirements: the document itself says that later specifications for routing, prefix management, security, naming and service discovery are expected to observe them.

sections.title: What the Home Network Has to Become
sections.content:
Home networks are growing in two directions at once. More devices are being connected, through an increasingly broad range of media, and more of the traffic is crossing internal routers rather than staying on a single flat network. Most homes today are still simple: one subnet, IPv4, provisioned by the provider, often with private addressing and cascading network address translation, and sometimes needing expert help to set up.

IPv6 changes that. A home can be given enough address space for every device to have a globally unique address, and for a prefix to be set aside for each internal subnet, so separate networks for guests, for home automation, or for a worker's company extension become possible. That in turn means the home needs internal routing, and it means the provider has to delegate a block large enough to hand out a prefix per subnet.

It is not realistic to expect the people living in the house to configure any of this, so the document's basic assumption is that the home network is as far as possible self-organising and self-configuring, working without the resident managing it, while still allowing an advanced user to adjust the result. The scope is the network layer: addressing, connectivity, routing, naming and service discovery. Physical, wireless and data link considerations are left out, and the design of a home router from top to bottom is not specified.

Whatever the topology, the home network has to be able to provide routing, prefix configuration for routers, name resolution, service discovery and network security. Those five are the backbone of the rest of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Homes are filling with devices, and many of those devices now talk through an internal router instead of sharing one flat network. IPv6 makes several subnets practical, but only if the network can set itself up without the people living there doing the work. The document lists the five jobs the network must do and then works through each one.

sections.title: Topologies, Multihoming and Self-Organisation
sections.content:
There should be no built-in assumption about how the home is wired, because users connect equipment in ingenious ways. Arbitrary topologies and arbitrary routing must be supported, or at least the failure must be as graceful as possible, for example by deactivating the part of the network that is causing trouble so that the rest keeps working, and by telling the user what happened. No topology should lose connectivity unless the user has created a physical island. Bridging two ports of a router together can be detected and dealt with, and loops in a routed topology are not harmful because they provide redundancy.

Several properties describe any home network and its operation: whether internal routers are present, whether there are isolated internal subnets with no direct connectivity between them, whether the provider or the customer manages the customer edge router, how many upstream providers there are, and how many customer edge routers there are. The last two matter because a home with two providers needs the network to handle both prefixes at once, and because more than one customer edge router adds complexity for protocols such as the Port Control Protocol, which manage connection state on the same router as later traffic flows.

The network should also be self-organising under different conditions of connectivity, device count and physical layout, while still letting an advanced user override the result. Manual steps are sometimes unavoidable, for example entering a cryptographic key for wireless security or a shared routing secret, and the number of such steps should be as small as possible. Two further points matter. Self-configuration must not pull in unintended devices: there should be a simple way for the owner to state whether a device belongs to the home, and pairing is suggested, for example by pressing buttons on two devices at the same time. And the network has to know where its own site ends, which defines the border for unique local addresses and for site-scope multicast, and usually there are internal borders too, such as a guest realm. A simple model has three realms, the internal home network, the provider, and a guest network, with a border between each pair, and more can be added.
sections.plainLanguage: The document refuses to assume any particular wiring. Whatever boxes the resident plugs together, the network should keep working, and if it cannot, it should say so and disable only the part that is at fault. It also insists the network can tell its own devices from a neighbour's, and that the point where the home stops and the provider begins is a defined border where the security rules apply.

sections.title: Prefixes and Stable Internal Addresses
sections.content:
A home may be offered a prefix of any length, such as a /60, a /56 or a /48, and the home has to adapt without assuming the prefix will be stable or long. The document quotes the guidance that end sites should always be able to obtain a reasonable amount of address space, in practice at least one /64 and in most cases significantly more, and it asks the customer edge router to request a /48 by DHCP Prefix Delegation, the largest prefix it might expect, even if it is only offered a /56 or a /60. It is not recommended that a provider offer less than a /60, and a /56 is highly preferable. If only a /64 is offered, the home is severely constrained or unable to function, and rather than contrive a workaround the receiving router should enter an error state and warn.

Renumbering is treated as a normal event. A provider may restructure and renumber its customers, and this is likely to be a flash renumbering, a sudden change rather than a graceful transition through two active prefixes. Where local law requires prefix changes for privacy, a non-flag-day process may be possible. A customer who changes provider should expect a discontinuity, and the prefix length may change too. The requirement is that homenet protocols support rapid renumbering without adding complexity, and that internal operation does not depend on the provider's network being up, except for reaching services outside the home.

That last point is why Unique Local Addresses are central. A home should use ULAs alongside its global prefixes so that devices on different subnets can talk to each other with addresses that do not change when the provider renumbers, and so that the home keeps working during an outage. ULAs should be used for all devices, not only those meant to stay internal, and default address selection then prefers them for internal traffic. Unlike private IPv4 space, the use of ULAs does not imply a NAT: a node with both a ULA and a global address should use the ULA internally and the global address for external traffic, and neither IPv6 NAT nor prefix translation is recommended for the home. The border routers should filter packets with ULA addresses so that they do not leave the home.

Inside the home, prefixes are then delegated further. The mechanism should not assume a flat or hierarchical model, nor whether assignment is distributed or centralised, and it should give each link a prefix that survives reboots and short outages, independent of the order in which routers start. Where ULAs are used, one /48 covering the whole home is preferable, from which /64s are handed out to subnets, and where two /48 ULAs exist the network must still work, with hosts knowing that each ULA is local.
sections.plainLanguage: The home asks its provider for a big block of addresses and then cuts it into pieces, one per subnet. The document asks for a /48 and says a provider should never give less than a /60. Separately, every device also gets an address of its own that never changes, so that a printer or a lamp keeps working when the provider renumbers the home or when the provider's network is down.

sections.title: Routing and Multicast Inside the Home
sections.content:
Routing inside the home is needed once there is more than one router, and it might be as simple as the current IPv4 model where the default route is up, or it might involve a routing protocol. A mechanism is required to discover which router is providing the customer edge function, because a border may be the interface to the provider, a gateway to a separate low-power network, or a gateway to a guest or corporate extension network, and in some cases there may be no border at all, for example before the upstream connection is established.

The routing environment should be self-configuring, and the self-configuration process and the routing protocol must interact predictably during startup and reconvergence. Configuration information is preferably distributed and synchronised by a separate protocol. The routing protocol should be based on one already deployed and shown to be reliable and robust, while allowing a newer protocol once a good open source implementation exists; the code must fit lightweight implementations and consumer devices, where memory, storage and processing are scarce. At most one unicast and one multicast routing protocol should be in use at a time in a given home, and where routers support more than one, a mechanism must ensure they all agree.

The unicast protocol's job is to give good enough end-to-end connectivity often enough, as defined by user expectations. Because the home mixes link technologies, path selection may benefit from being more refined than hop count, and traffic may do better over several paths than over one. Convergence should be quick, no slower than the outages users are used to when the customer edge router reboots. The protocol should support several internet connections and several delegated prefixes at once, and making routing decisions from source as well as destination addresses is highly desirable, to avoid problems with upstream ingress filtering. It must not need the provider's connection in order to keep routing inside the home. Low-power networks and other specialised networks are treated as stub areas, not transit for other traffic.

Multicast across the home is desirable, including source-specific multicast, both for home-wide service discovery and for streaming and file sharing. The border with the provider must be administratively configured, as the addressing architecture requires for any boundary of scope 4 or higher, and there may be other multicast borders, for example towards a guest subnet. Where multicast is routed, a multicast routing protocol is required, which should also be self-configuring, and multicast must be scoped or filtered so that it is not flooded onto media whose devices cannot support it.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the home has more than one router, something has to tell the routers about the others, and that has to happen without the resident doing anything. The document wants the routing protocol to be one that is already proven, small enough for cheap consumer equipment, and able to work out which way to send traffic from the source address as well as the destination, so that a home with two providers still works.

sections.title: Security: Addressable Is Not Reachable
sections.content:
The biggest change from the IPv4 model is that the NAT is gone and devices are globally addressable, so it has to be decided whether they should be globally reachable. The document asks the architecture to embrace end-to-end transparency: each device should be globally addressable and its addresses must not be altered in transit, but security perimeters can still restrict who may talk to whom, so a host may be addressable without being reachable.

What the default should be is unresolved. A default deny policy would replace the need for IPv4 NAT traversal protocols with the need to ask the firewall to open a hole, for example with the Port Control Protocol, and in a home with several customer edge routers the signalling would have to handle flows that leave through more than one of them. The recommendations on perimeter security state that a transparent mode must be available so that a default allow model remains possible. The document makes no recommendation beyond that, because the choice may be situational, but it does ask that the option of running in default deny mode should be kept, since the implicit firewall of an IPv4 NAT is commonplace today.

Filtering is also wanted at internal borders, so that a guest can reach a printer but not the rest of the home, and the policies must be easy enough for a typical user to apply. The document is careful about how much a firewall can be relied on: obscurity and filtering are at best partially effective, since a compromise behind the firewall exposes everything else, and a home network that relies on either is as vulnerable as its weakest device. Given the poor default security of many devices, keeping the perimeter defence is still worthwhile, and hosts should also apply their own security policies according to their capabilities, with a way to ask for traffic to be allowed through the home's filters.

Two further points are raised. With service discovery across the whole home, there is a risk that devices leak information to vendors or application providers, and the threat should at least be recognised. And because the border filters unique local addresses, a ULA source address can be taken as an indication of traffic from inside the home, which can be used with security settings to decide which nodes an application may talk to.
sections.plainLanguage: Giving every device a global address means anyone on the internet can try to reach it, so the home needs a border where traffic is filtered. The document does not settle whether that border should block everything by default or allow everything by default, because people disagree and the right choice depends on the home. It does insist the option of blocking by default must remain available.

sections.title: Naming and Service Discovery
sections.content:
The home network needs devices to be reachable by names that no other device on the network uses, and users and devices need to find the services available, such as media servers, printers, displays and automation devices. The service that provides this must work without management by the resident. It has to work whether the user is inside or outside the home, and the natural way to think about it is that it covers the whole site, ignoring technical borders such as subnets but respecting policy borders such as the one between a guest network and the rest of the home. Remote access by the residents while travelling may also be wanted, and possibly by manufacturers or other third parties.

The home name service should support both lookups, which query a known service, and discovery, which may use multicast messages or a service where applications register to be found. It must at least coexist with the Internet name service, and there should be a bias towards proven solutions, which points to a DNS-based or DNS-compatible service. There are protocols built for the wider internet, such as unicast DNS, and protocols built for zero-configuration local use, such as Multicast DNS. Where DNS is used, it typically has a resolving service and an authoritative service that hosts the home's zone; one approach is to run the authoritative service on the customer edge router with a secondary one provided by the provider or another party, which makes resolution from the global internet possible.

Where a global name space is in use, devices should be able to add entries to it, and there should be a way to remove or expire them. To protect against cache poisoning, name service security methods such as the DNS Security Extensions should be supported on both the authoritative server and the resolver side, and the home router must not prevent DNSSEC from working. Devices supporting DNSSEC need good random number generation. If a global name space is not available, the home uses a local one, which has meaning only inside the home. Finally, replacing the customer edge router must not lose the configuration: the relevant state should be distributed within the home, or handed to the provider or an external service, so that the new router can recover it.
sections.plainLanguage: People should be able to reach a printer by name, and a phone in the house should be able to find a speaker without being told where it is. The document wants that to work across every subnet in the home while still keeping a guest network out of it, and it wants the naming system to be based on DNS so that it does not clash with the rest of the internet. It also wants the home's own names protected against forgery, which means the DNS security extensions have to work inside the home.

items.text: From the prefix the provider delegates to the home.

items.text: A private address of the home's own, used for internal traffic.

items.title: Privacy address
items.text: A temporary address used so the device is harder to track.

items.text: Present as well when the home runs both address families.
